title: Self-Defining Memories in Head and Neck Cancer Patients and Control Group
abstract: Objective This exploratory study examined whether self-defining memories (SDM) differ in specificity, integration, and emotional valence between individuals treated for head and neck cancer (HNC) and matched controls. An exploratory thematic analysis examined cancer-related SDM. Methods Twenty-one patients with HNC and 22 controls reported five SDM each (215 memories). Memories were coded for specificity, integration, emotional valence, and thematic content. Intraclass correlation coefficients and multilevel logistic regression models examined group differences and associations between emotional valence and integration. Cancer-related SDM were additionally examined thematically. Results No group differences were found in specificity or integration (ps > .80). Positive and mixed SDM were more likely to be integrated than negative or neutral SDM. Four themes emerged: diagnostic uncertainty and delays; cancer diagnosis and disclosure; interpersonal relationships and cancer; and consequences of HNC treatment. Conclusions SDM integration was associated with emotional valence rather than cancer status. Qualitative findings highlighted diverse and personally meaningful representations of cancer experiences.
